Gambela Region, Ethiopia · data pack for a flood- and drought-safe toilet · built 15–16 Nov 2026

Gambella: floods, drought, money, toilets and safety

Every number in the tables comes from a named source file in gambella/data/. Text marked my analysis is Claude's own calculation or interpretation, not a statement from a source.

Summary my analysis

50%of people live in cells where a 100-year flood covers ≥10% of the cell
74%of people live between 400 and 500 m elevation
47%open defecation in 2024 (DHS) — no progress since 2016 (45%)
52%of people live on swelling-clay Vertisols
29flood/drought events found 1961–2025 (24 floods)
438,572registered refugees in Gambella (UNHCR data portal, 31 Oct 2026) — mostly missing from population maps
  • Flood, not drought, is the hazard where people live. About half the host population lives where the 100-year river flood reaches; 32% where it covers at least half the cell. Elevation and flood extent are strongly negatively related (ρ = -0.75 across cells, -0.90 across 0.25° blocks).
  • Drought likelihood depends on how you measure it. The lowland plain is drier on average (dry months vs elevation ρ = -0.92), but years with rain below 80% of normal are rare everywhere (0–18% of years) and cluster in the thinly populated south. Population density is negatively related to that drought measure (ρ = -0.34).
  • Elevation vs population: weakly negative (ρ = -0.37 cells, -0.23 blocks, not significant). Most people are on the plain, but the eastern highland woredas Godere and Mengesh are also dense.
  • Income does not explain toilet progress. Across regions richer means better sanitation (ρ = 0.86), but within a region, income growth and sanitation gains are unrelated (ρ = 0.00). In 2019 Gambela had the 4th-highest open defecation of 11 regions despite middling income.
  • Safety: sexual and partner violence is common in camps and Gambella town (35–59% in local studies); DHS figures are much lower and known to undercount. Studies elsewhere link open-air or shared toilets to higher odds of non-partner sexual violence (odds ratios about 1.2–2.5). No study measures latrine-related violence in Gambella itself.

Ethiopia as a whole (EM-DAT): 63 flood and 18 drought records 1965–2026; 6,775,672 people affected by floods and 108,041,879 by droughts (summed over records). EM-DAT carries no place names, so it cannot be filtered to Gambella.

Rainfall against the records my analysis

  • Wetter years are much more likely to have a recorded flood (ρ = 0.62, 1981–2025).
  • Recorded droughts barely relate to rainfall (ρ = -0.16) or SPEI (ρ = -0.10); "drought" here is more about late rains and failed flood-recession farming than low annual totals.
  • Caution: rainfall has risen (year vs rain ρ = 0.49) while reporting improved, which inflates the flood link.

Economy and GDP

No official regional GDP exists for Gambella. What exists: national GDP (World Bank), modelled regional GNI and HDI (Global Data Lab), gridded GDP (Kummu et al.), and old JICA projections. All regional values below are modelled.

Regional poverty headcount (national poverty line, NPC 2017): 50.5% (1999/00) → 32% (2010/11) → 23.0% (2015/16).

Gambela's modelled GNI per capita (GDL, 2017 PPP $) rose from 864 (2000) to 2,987 (2023), and its HDI from 0.356 to 0.546.

Reported risks (qualitative)

  • Women and girls face harassment, physical attacks and rape where they collect firewood/water (Pagak reception centre) (Pagak reception centre, Gambella, 2020.0; UN agency / cluster report (qualitative); checked: ✓ yes)
  • Lack of lighting around camps enhances SGBV risk at night when accessing services; street lighting proposed for water points and communal latrines (Ethiopia refugee camps incl. Gambella, 2018.0; UN agency / cluster report (qualitative); checked: ✗ no)
  • Women moving long distances on foot to fetch water at heightened risk of GBV; basic GBV services not yet provided (flood-displaced IDPs) (Lare, Jikawo and Wanthoa woredas (Nuer Zone), 2025.0; UN agency / cluster report (qualitative); checked: ✓ yes)
  • Limited protection partners and budget delays disrupting referral of GBV survivors to the One-Stop Center (Gambella (conflict/drought affected areas), 2025.0; UN agency / cluster report (qualitative); checked: ✗ no)
  • FGDs: women and girls exposed to higher risk of sexual, physical and psychological violence at firewood collection sites; in Gambella unmet basic needs (clothes, shoes, food) raise exploitation risk for adolescent girls (Ethiopia refugee operations incl. Where to improve sanitation first my analysis

There is no village-level toilet data: DHS gives one number for the whole region. So this map ranks places by how many people live where ordinary pit latrines are most likely to fail (river flood, swelling clay, long dry season). Weights and thresholds are my choice; the robustness map shows the result holds under other weights.
220kpeople in high-priority cells (score ≥ 0.6) of 640k host population
211kpeople where only a raised or sealed above-ground toilet makes sense (zone A)
161cells (278k people) in the top 20% under all four weightings

How to read it

  • Start in Jikawo, Wantawo and Lare: almost everyone there lives in the top priority band, and nearly all of it is zone A (raised/sealed units). Akobo and Itang follow.
  • Zone A: a 10-year flood covers ≥30% or a 100-year flood ≥50% of the cell. Pits will be flooded.
  • Zone B: flood edge (100-year flood 10–50%). Raised slab over a lined pit.
  • Zone C: little river flooding, but clay soils. Lined pit; plan for dry-season water.
  • Gambella town and the big camps (Nguenyiel, Tierkidi, Kule) fall in zones B/C on this river-flood model, but the model does not include flooding from heavy rain on flat clay ground; the camps' own flood history (2014) says to check on site.
  • Camps hold about 370,000 refugees missing from the population layer, so they rank too low here. Treat them as a separate priority.

What this means for the toilet design my analysis

  • Design for floods first. Most people live on the flat 400–450 m plain that the Baro, Gilo and Akobo flood. A pit that floods spreads faeces; the 2014 camp floods made latrines overflow and collapse. Raised or sealed units suit the western woredas (Jikawo, Wantawo, Lare, Akobo, Jor).
  • Expect swelling clay. Vertisols crack in the dry season and turn to mud when wet; unlined pits slump. Linings and bases need to cope with ground that moves.
  • Drought matters for water, less for structure. The plain has about five dry months a year; designs needing flush water will fail then. Dry or low-water designs fit better.
  • Owning is not using. In one study 47% of households with a latrine still practised open defecation, and open defecation stayed at about 45–47% while income rose. Comfort, privacy and maintenance matter as much as cost.
  • Safety features are evidence-based elsewhere, unproven here. Locks, lighting, separate women's units and placement close to the home address the risks named in camp surveys (missing locks, no separate men's/women's latrines, night-time use). No study measures their effect in Gambella; that would need your own survey.
  • Count refugees separately. About 439,000 refugees live largely outside the population map, in camps with 6–64 people per latrine.

Data quality

Every data file was re-checked on 16 Nov 2026 by an independent checker that re-opened the cited sources. Rows marked "wrong" are kept so the problem stays visible.

Errors found and fixed

  • 2007 flood: IFRC's 36,090 affected was a five-region total; Gambella's share is 20,000.
  • 2007 flood: Dartmouth figures (42,000 displaced, 17 dead) cover most of Ethiopia; the yearly value now uses Gambella sources (11,886 displaced, 1 death).
  • Population grid: a 0.1° westward shift was fixed (regional total 816,595 → 645,689).
  • Bandyopadhyay 2023: effect size −0.006 (not −0.005); sample size 76,580 added.

Still uncertain

  • 11,749 displaced may belong to 2020, not 2021 (the OCHA original sits behind a bot check).
  • The two 2024 flood entries may be the same season counted twice.
  • 1998: 66,000 displaced rests on a map match only. 2019: sources differ about eightfold (1,405 vs 11,128 displaced).
  • Two modelled population series disagree (480,000 vs 610,000 in 2022). WorldPop misses camp refugees.
  • Flood extent is a global model (JRC); groundwater depth was not found in any dataset.
  • Sources not accessed: ReliefWeb/OCHA (bot check), EDRMC/NDRMC sites (no response), several news sites (403).

Files and sources

Folder: OneDrive/Research/gambella/ — data/ CSVs (UTF-8, each row with source, URL and year), maps/ PNGs, scripts/ to rebuild, raw/ downloads, README.md index.

Main sources: DHS Program API (2000–2024 surveys); World Bank API; Global Data Lab sub-national HDI; Kummu et al. gridded GDP; EM-DAT via Our World in Data; IFRC GO; GDACS; Dartmouth Flood Observatory; UNHCR, UNICEF and Protection Cluster reports; peer-reviewed studies via Europe PMC; Copernicus DEM GLO-90; WorldPop 2020 (1 km, UN-adjusted); ISRIC SoilGrids 2.0; CHIRPS v2.0 rainfall; CHC SPEI-12; JRC Global Surface Water; JRC global river flood hazard maps; geoBoundaries and OCHA COD-AB boundaries; OSM waterways.

EM-DAT data are for non-commercial use; publish aggregated counts only.
